**Verdict:** Yes, and this rests mostly on Graham's essays, not on the vault. As I know his position, he would tell you to move to Silicon Valley, at least for the early, fragile stage. The reason isn't that Stockholm lacks talent. It's that a startup is more likely to die in a place without many investors, experienced founders and people who take startups seriously.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault. Graham never addresses where founders should be based in any of the 10 sources in `yc-pre`, so I can't quote him on it. What follows is labelled by where it comes from.

**What he's written elsewhere (not in the vault)**
- His essay *Why to Move to a Startup Hub* (2007, paulgraham.com) argues that startups succeed far more often in hubs, because outside one they die more easily. Away from a hub you lack investors, people who have done it before, and an environment that treats what you're doing as normal. He says this directly.
- *Cities and Ambition* (2008) argues that every city sends a message about what matters, and Silicon Valley's is about building powerful things. You absorb whatever message your city sends.
- *Why Startups Condense in America* (2006) is about why Europe produces fewer startups. Its reasons include investors who are cautious about funding them and attitudes toward failure.
- YC's practice matches this. For years the program required founders to come to the Bay Area for the batch.

These are paraphrases from memory, not quotes. Check the essays themselves before you rely on the exact wording.

**What the vault does show**
- In *Superlinear Returns*, Graham describes Silicon Valley's culture of betting on founders who learn from failure: "This is one reason Silicon Valley is so tolerant of failure. People in Silicon Valley aren't blindly tolerant of failure. They'll only continue to bet on you if you're learning from your failures." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]], https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html). That describes the environment. He doesn't use it to argue that you have to move there.
- **What they did (Livingston's account, not Graham's words):** YC started in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Within months they moved it to Silicon Valley. In 2024 Livingston recalls Graham saying "in like September oh we have to do this out in Silicon Valley" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 21:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=1293s). Her 2018 talk gives the reason: "we didn't want someone else to be the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley, we wanted to be that ourselves" ([[yt-8d-cApFHjeY]] @ 12:02, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=722s). Boston already had Harvard and MIT, and they still decided Silicon Valley was the place to be.

**What might change his answer:** His argument is about how fragile startups are early on. Once you have traction, revenue and investors, staying put matters less. Stockholm is also stronger than most European cities: Spotify and Klarna started there, and it has investors who have been through it. I don't know of anything where he exempts Stockholm specifically.

**My own view:** The pull of a hub has probably weakened since 2007, with remote work and funding available in Europe. Graham's argument is still a reasonable default for a first-time founder.

The vault has no Graham source on this question. If you want it answered from cited sources, add *Why to Move to a Startup Hub* and *Cities and Ambition* to the vault and compile them.

**Verdict:** No. Paul Graham would tell you to win on product. A brand is what you get after you've made something people love. If you try to build the brand first, you're "playing house": copying how a successful company looks while skipping the one thing that makes it successful.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from PG on "brand vs. product" as such. His view on tricks versus substance settles the question anyway.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Users are the only judges, and they judge the product.** "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right?" ([Before the Startup, 2014](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s) @ 12:10). And: "you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extent that you do." (@ 12:43)
- **Positioning tricks are minor.** "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s)). Applied to brand: a brand without a product behind it is one of those tricks.
- **His growth formula puts product first.** "The way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." ([@ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s)). Telling people about it is the brand's job, and it comes second. In the same passage: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit."
- **Brand matters, but as something that compounds once you're winning.** In *Superlinear Returns* (2023) he lists brand as work that compounds: "doing well in one cycle causes you to do better in the next. That happens for example when you're building infrastructure, or growing an audience or brand" ([paulgraham.com/superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). So he doesn't dismiss brand. It multiplies a product that's already good. It doesn't stand in for one.
- **When you go after an incumbent, the opening is a better product.** "If a company makes a product that people dislike yet still buy, then presumably they'd buy a better alternative if you made one." (same essay). Seibel and Caldwell (2022) say the same about Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe: none of them were first, and each won by being 10x better than bad incumbents ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8)).

**One nuance from YC, though not from PG:** at 14:46 of that 2022 video, Caldwell or Seibel (the transcript doesn't say which) calls Stripe's "really clever brand promise" an effort to "make the most beautiful website they could with the most beautiful documentation". The brand people cite as a success came from the quality of the product.

**What would change his answer:** the vault doesn't say. My guess, outside the vault: once a startup has a product people love, he'd be fine with investing in brand as compounding work. He'd still say no to brand as the way into a market.

**The vault can't answer this.** Sam Altman is listed as a member of `vaults/yc-pre` (`vault.yaml:18`), but none of the vault's sources are by him. No quote in the wiki is attributed to him, and he doesn't speak in the raw transcripts. He only comes up in other people's words: Livingston saying "Sam Altman was impressive at age 19" ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 54:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=3274s)), and PG addressing "Sam" while giving a lecture in his 2014 Stanford class. Nothing in the vault touches his views on AI.

Below is my best answer from public statements outside the vault. It's paraphrased, not quoted.

**Verdict:** The future that worries Altman most is a quiet one, not killer robots. People and institutions come to rely on AI so much that they hand it their decisions, and humanity loses control without anyone choosing to give it up.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault

**What he has said (not in the vault)**
- **2025, his most recent framing:** He named three scary scenarios. A bad actor gets superintelligence first and uses it for things like bioweapons or attacks on the power grid or financial system. AI goes rogue and won't be shut off. And AI "accidentally" takes over because society depends on it too much, such as a leader who can't act without asking ChatGPT. He spends the most time on the third, and has called it "really bad" that young people say they can't make a life decision without consulting ChatGPT.
- **2023, Senate testimony:** He said his worst fear was that the AI industry causes "significant harm to the world."
- **2023, interview:** He said the worst case is "lights out for all of us." In the short term, though, he worried more about accidental misuse than about AI turning hostile.
- **Recurring theme:** Over time his focus has moved from sudden disaster toward slow harm to society: dependence, reduced human agency, and power ending up concentrated.

**Closest view inside the vault:** Paul Graham, not Altman, worries about a related loss of human ability. In *Writes and Write-Nots* (2024) he predicts AI will leave few people able to write, and since writing is thinking, fewer people who can think clearly ([web-14f0078fb455](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html); wiki page `writing/ai-and-writing/writing-is-thinking`).

**To make the vault answer this properly:** add Altman's own sources (his blog at blog.samaltman.com, his interviews and his testimony) to `vault.yaml`, then discover, curate and compile them.

I can do that next, or save this answer to `derived/`.

**Verdict:** Seibel would tell you to stop. Months spent on a deck and on follow-up meetings means fundraising has replaced building the company. Go back to putting the product in front of users and getting customers, because traction is what raises money, not polish.

**Based on:** Follows from what he said. The vault has no Seibel talk about fundraising itself, so this applies his MVP and launch advice, plus one line about investors, to your situation. One point at the end comes from outside the vault and is labelled that way.

**Why he'd say it**
- **He compared deck time with build time directly.** "So spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([Seibel, *How to Plan an MVP*, 2019 @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))
- **Only customers tell you whether it works.** "If you put the thing in front of them and it doesn't solve their problem, you know right away." He adds that until then "you have no faking idea whether it's going to work" (same talk @ 10:39–11:11). A follow-up meeting with an investor can't tell you that.
- **He doesn't treat investor opinions as a signal about your product.** He warns against changing course because "god forbid, you talk to an investor and they say, 'Oh, that could never be a company.' Because investors know everything." (@ 11:44, said sarcastically). Months of investor feedback can quietly reshape your plan the same way.
- **A "no" from investors doesn't mean the idea is bad.** On Coinbase: "he had a impossible time raising money on demo day and so if he had taken the demo day signal the investor signal of oh we don't want to give you money and quit we don't have coinbase" ([Seibel/Caldwell 2022 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s)). The vault isn't sure whether Seibel or Caldwell said this. So the rejections don't mean you should quit. They mean pitching harder isn't the fix.
- **YC's general view, from PG, matches his.** "Someone who knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money. Than someone who knows every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph." ([PG 2014 @ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))

**What he'd tell you to do instead:** Redefine your "launch" as "when you get any customers" and get there in weeks. Time-box the spec, write it down, cut it. Then go back to investors with a usage graph instead of a better deck.

**What would change his answer:** The vault gives one exception. In "heavy MVP" fields like biotech, hardware or regulated finance, you may truly need capital before customers can use anything. Even then he'd want the smallest thing you can show, such as a website.

**Beyond the vault (not in the vault):** Seibel's public fundraising advice generally treats raising as a short, compressed process rather than months of open-ended meetings. He also says a slow or vague investor response is usually a no. I'm fairly confident of that, but none of his fundraising-specific talks are in this vault. They would be worth adding if you want quotes for it.

My own view, in one line: this is good advice if you have no traction. If you already have strong growth and still can't close, the problem may be how you run the raise, and the vault doesn't cover that.

**Verdict:** No. Caldwell would say that "safe" usually means the idea *sounds* sensible to the people around you, and that's a poor guide. The ideas he's watched work, Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe, all looked scary, small or "gnarly" at the start. A modest-looking idea doesn't improve your odds. It mostly moves you closer to the consensus.

**Based on:** follows from what they said. The vault has no Caldwell quote about "modest vs. ambitious" ideas. His view comes from the 2022 talk with Michael Seibel, *Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?* ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8)).

**Why he'd say it**
- **Ideas that looked risky or bad are the ones that won.** He lists what people thought at the time. Airbnb: "Renting a room in a house with a host there was like the ultimate unappealing, scary, bad thing that no one wanted to do." ([@ 4:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=297s)). Coinbase: "People saw bitcoin as a tiny market, that it was going to crash, that it was a bubble." ([@ 9:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=590s)), and "Getting a bank deal was impossible." ([@ 10:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=623s)). He admits he got it wrong himself: he thought Airbnb "kind of felt like the third-rate entrant to a crowded space at the time." ([@ 1:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=98s)).
- **A hard problem is an opening, not something to avoid.** On accepting credit cards before Stripe: "It's a possible thing to do, but I would call it gnarly and the opposite of easy in every way." ([@ 13:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=788s)). That pain is why a product 10x better than what existed could win.
- **People tend to aim too low, not too high.** Even Brian Armstrong underrated Coinbase: "Even Brian in his YC application didn't really believe in his own idea." ([@ 10:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=623s)). Simply letting people buy bitcoin safely "was enough" ([@ 10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=656s)). Seibel's conclusion in the same talk: "Be very careful about your initial market math," and "Don't be discouraged if someone's like, that's a tiny market." ([@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1182s), [@ 20:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1216s)).
- **The real safety check is users, not how plausible the idea sounds.** Their test is whether the problem is one you or your peers have, and whether the existing options are bad. Seibel says you shouldn't care what experts think, "especially... if they're not going to be users" ([@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1182s)).

**What he's done:** He set up merchant accounts himself in 2002 and 2007, then joined Stripe's beta as one of its first hundred customers. He skipped buying bitcoin around 2011 because buying it looked like a scam. His record shows him learning, through his own mistakes, that "looks risky" and "is bad" are different things.

**What would change his answer:** The talk's test is whether you and your peers actually have the problem and hate the current options. If the "safe" idea passes that test, it's fine. If the "ambitious" idea doesn't, it isn't. Not in the vault, and from memory: Caldwell has a separate YC talk on "tarpit ideas." These sound easy and appealing, so many founders try them, but they keep failing for structural reasons. In his view those "safe-feeling" ideas are a trap.

One caveat from me: the talk only looks at three huge winners in hindsight. It shows that good ideas often look bad, not that ideas that look bad are usually good.

**Verdict:** The vault can't answer this. Nothing in it records Garry Tan saying anything about who owns AI agent workflows or skill files, or about AI agents at all.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault (and here, mostly a guess)

**What the vault has on Tan**
- He appears in one source, the 2024 Lightcone episode "How YC Was Created" ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY). He's a host interviewing Jessica Livingston there, so most of what he says is questions, not opinions.
- The profile calls him a YC partner and investor who promotes YC, and notes he mentions his own fund, Initialized ([[yt-6u4JVz7iQTY]] @ 40:30).
- I searched the wiki and the raw transcripts for ownership, employer/IP, agents, AI, skills and workflows. Nothing relevant came up from Tan or from any other member.

**My best guess (not in the vault):** Tan probably thinks it matters, and would want you to treat the skills you build as your own compounding asset. Since 2025 he has talked publicly, and a lot, about building with AI coding agents. I believe he has also open-sourced his own Claude Code setup and skills ("gstack"), but I haven't checked that against a source. If that's right, his own practice is to keep skills portable and public, not locked inside one employer. I don't have a statement from him on employer ownership, so don't quote me as quoting him.

**Practical note (mine, not Tan's):** Who actually owns what you build at work depends on your employment contract's IP-assignment clause. It doesn't depend on any investor's opinion. Check it before you assume your skill files are yours to take with you.

The vault's name ("pre") suggests its sources stop before 2026, which is probably why Tan's agent-era views aren't in it. To get a cited answer, add his own channel content from 2025–2026 (e.g. `@garrytan`, already listed in `vault.yaml`) and re-run discover, curate, fetch and compile.

**Verdict:** No. Launch now with a cut-down version and treat the request list as input, not a to-do list. Seibel's rule is "launch something bad quickly", and in his terms you're past the deadline: the plan for an MVP is weeks, and you're at three months without launching.

**Based on:** Seibel said it directly. Applying it to feature requests from user calls follows from what he said. The vault has nothing from Caldwell on launching or feature requests, so his part below is thin.

**Why Michael would say it** ([2019 "How to Plan an MVP"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM))
- **Launching is the job.** "If you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." ([@ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)) He also warns: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s))
- **An MVP is weeks of work, not months.** "You should be able to build it fast in weeks, not months." Focus on "a small set of initial users and their highest order problems and then ignore the rest until later." (@ 4:29–5:03)
- **What you're describing is the trap he names.** "Your three-week plan turns into a three-month plan." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s)) His fix is to time-box the spec ("the only things that could be on my spec are things I can build in three weeks") and then cut it: "Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important... if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things." ([@ 12:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=737s))
- **Your bar for "launched" is too high.** "How about launch is when you get any customers." ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s)) If someone on those calls wants the product, give it to them this week.
- **Requests made on calls are weaker evidence than use.** "It's a lot harder to learn from your customers when they don't have a product they can play with. If you put the thing in front of them and it doesn't solve their problem, you know right away." ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s)) And: "It might turn out the full thing that you want to build isn't what your customers want at all." ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s))
- **Don't get attached to the feature set.** "Hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." (@ 3:19) And: "You wouldn't fall in love with a paper you wrote in the first grade and like that's like the level of impact often your MVP has." ([@ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s))
- **The famous companies launched without obvious features.** Airbnb had no payments and Stripe had "almost no features". "All of these are billion-dollar companies and they all started with something that most people would say is pretty shitty." (@ 5:37–7:52) In his 2022 talk with Caldwell, Seibel adds that Airbnb found its key missing feature, payments, by using the product after launch, not by planning it beforehand ([2022 talk @ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=264s)).

**Dalton:** Nothing in the vault from him covers this. His only material is the 2022 ideas talk, where he praises Stripe for focusing hard on one customer: "They went nuts at making something that developers would just freak out about." ([@ 15:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=918s)) Applied to your case, that means getting one type of user to love the product, not covering everything everyone asks for. That's my inference from the principle, not something he said about feature requests.

**What would change Michael's answer:** a regulated or hard-tech product, such as insurance, banking, biotech or rockets. In those he allows a "heavy MVP", though even then he says to start with a simple website (@ 7:52–8:59). Nothing you've said suggests you're in that category.

**Applied to you (my extrapolation):** Claude Code makes building cheap, so following every request feels free. Seibel's argument is about learning, not about how much building costs: until people are using the product, you don't know which requests matter. A practical way to apply his advice:
1. From the requests, pick the single problem that keeps coming up across calls.
2. Cut everything else from what you ship. Leave the code in place, just hidden.
3. Put the product in front of the people you've been talking to within days.
4. Build next only what their actual use shows they need.

One caveat: his examples are billion-dollar survivors, and the vault's profile notes the advice ignores lean launches that went nowhere. That doesn't help the case for waiting, though.

**Verdict:** I can't quote Michael Seibel on this. The yc-pre vault has nothing from him on cofounder breakups, equity or legal disputes. His sources there are only a 2019 talk on MVPs and a 2022 talk on startup ideas. Based on what YC generally advises, I think he'd tell you both to stop the lawyer letters, settle it between the two of you quickly, and spend your time on whatever comes next.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault. Everything below is my read, not his quotes.

**Why I think he'd say it (not in the vault)**
- **Your first sentence decides most of this.** If the company is over and neither of you wants to continue, the shares of a pre-PMF company that is shutting down are worth roughly nothing. Two sets of lawyers trading letters cost real money every week to fight over that. Dissolve the company, split whatever is left according to the documents, and move on.
- **If one of you wants to keep the company going, then the stake does matter.** A departed cofounder holding a large vested share is "dead equity." Investors push back on it, and it makes later fundraising harder. Usually the fix is a negotiated buyback or a smaller stake. You get there by the two of you agreeing on a number, with the lawyers writing up the result instead of arguing it.
- **YC's standard terms exist for this situation.** That's four-year vesting with a one-year cliff, and under a standard cliff nobody owns any vested shares at 9 months. Before arguing any further, read what your vesting agreement actually says. Did it have a cliff? Is there acceleration? Did the company keep a repurchase right? That language probably settles more than the letters will. I'm not a lawyer; your counsel should confirm what the documents mean.
- **His theme in the vault is that what counts is shipping to users.** He says things like "hold the problem you're solving tightly… hold the solution you're building loosely" ([video @ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s)). A long legal fight over a dead company is the opposite of where he tells founders to spend their time. This is a loose link, though. He said it about MVPs, not about breakups.

**What would change the answer:** if the company has real value (revenue, IP someone would buy, or money in the bank worth fighting over), the stake is real and having lawyers is reasonable. Even then, I'd expect his advice to be to negotiate a settlement fast rather than drag it out.

The vault does touch the topic elsewhere: Jessica Livingston says the cofounder relationship was the thing YC weighed "most importantly" when deciding whom to fund ([video @ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s)). If you want Seibel's own words on this, I can look for a YC source where he covers cofounder breakups and add it to the vault.

**The vault has nothing from Garry Tan on AI or agents.** His only statements in `yc-pre` are about YC fund returns ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=2430s) @ 40:30). So this answer is a labelled guess. It combines what I know of Tan from outside the vault with YC principles that other members did document.

**Verdict:** This week, pick one real problem that you or your users have. Have an agent build something for it, ship it, and spend your own hours driving the agent yourself. Don't read about agents or hand them off to someone else.

**Based on:** mostly beyond the vault, plus YC principles from PG and Seibel applied to this case.

**What Tan would likely say (not in the vault)**
- He's been one of the loudest YC voices for AI coding. In early 2025 he said about a quarter of the W25 batch had codebases that were roughly 95% AI-generated. He presents this as founders shipping far more with much smaller teams, and he codes with agents himself. His advice would be that founders get hands-on with the tools, not that they delegate the experiment.

**YC principles that apply (other members, in the vault)**
- **Start with your own problem.** Seibel: "It's even more helpful if you're your own user so you can tell whether your product's working for you." ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=33s) @ 0:33). Don't pick a demo task. Pick the workflow that annoys you most: support triage, a report, an internal tool, a feature on your backlog.
- **Time-box it and cut scope.** Seibel: "the only things that could be on my spec are things I can build in three weeks" (@ 11:11). Agents make the box shorter. Treat it as one week, and "if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things" (@ 12:17).
- **Ship it.** "Once you get anything out in the world, the momentum to keep anything going is extremely strong" (@ 12:17).
- **Get to the leading edge.** PG: "Get yourself to the leading edge of some technology, to, as Paul Buchheit put it, live in the future." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s) @ 29:06). Daily use is how you start seeing what "ought to exist" (@ 29:06), including startup ideas.

**A concrete week**
1. **Day 1:** Install one coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor or similar). Point it at a real repo or a blank one.
2. **Days 1–2:** Write a one-page spec for the problem you picked, and cut it in half.
3. **Days 2–5:** Build it with the agent. Your job is to review, test and redirect it.
4. **End of the week:** Put it in front of real users or your team. Write down what the agent did well, where it broke, and what you'd automate next.

**What would change the answer:** PG warns that outsourcing your writing means outsourcing your thinking: "writing is thinking" ([web-14f0078fb455](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)). Have agents do the building, but write the spec and make the product decisions yourself.

If you want answers in Tan's own words, the vault needs his sources. His YouTube channel is already configured, but none of his videos have been compiled. I can run `wwxd discover` and curate his AI-era videos.

**Verdict:** PG would push you on one question until you could answer it: which real user is trying to have an agent buy something *today*, failing, and wanting your product badly? "Agents will need to pay for things" is the kind of idea he warns sounds plausible but is often bad.

**Based on:** follows from what he said. Nothing in the vault covers AI agents or agentic payments. Every point below applies his general principles to your case, plus a few things I know about him that aren't in the vault, which I've labelled.

**What he'd push you on**

1. **Did you think this up, or did you run into it?** His warning about ideas you think up on purpose: "If you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s)). Infrastructure for agent commerce is plausible-sounding by default. So he'd ask where it came from. Are you running agents that keep getting stuck at checkout? The alternative he wants is to "live in the future" so that you notice things that "ought to exist" (@ [29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s)). Seibel says the same about Stripe: it was "a problem that they saw their peers in YC have" ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 14:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=854s)).

2. **Are you building a startup or acting like one?** His term for that is "playing house": founders copy what startups look like and neglect "the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." (@ [7:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s)). Infrastructure startups can easily ship SDKs, protocols, partnerships and a waitlist with nobody depending on any of it. He'd want names: which agent builders or merchants, and how many completed transactions last week. "There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want" (@ [12:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s)).

3. **Why is the current situation bad, and what keeps it that way?** He says a mediocre product that stays popular can be worth replacing, but "there's often a hidden reason why. Perhaps monopoly or regulation make it hard to compete." ([web-76d87c7c2e80](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). For you, the likely hidden reasons are card networks, merchants' bot and fraud defenses, and liability when an agent buys the wrong thing. He'd want you to say which one you're getting around and why you can. Seibel's test for a real insight: you're "the most expensive thing ... and people still are desperate for it." ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 16:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=985s)).

4. **Do things that don't scale. Pick a few users and integrate by hand.** He says to pay "a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers" ([web-76d87c7c2e80](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). Stripe is the obvious comparison: "No bank deals," and "the Stripe founders would come to your office and integrate it for you." ([yt-1hHMwLxN6EM @ 7:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=438s)). Payments is regulated, so it may feel like you need a "heavy MVP". Seibel's answer is to shrink scope anyway: one kind of agent, a small set of merchants, possibly a human approving purchases behind the scenes.

5. **What's your growth rate?** He'd ask for a weekly growth rate, not total volume, and he'd dismiss a pitch that rests on how big the market will be. "The best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)). He'd distrust distribution tricks too: "Whenever you hear anybody talk about growth hacks, just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." (@ [10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s)).

**Not in the vault:** his essays "Schlep Blindness" and "Do Things That Don't Scale" point the same way. Payments compliance and merchant integration are the tedious "schlep" (his word for a hard, unpleasant task) that keeps competitors out. He'd count it as a reason in your favor *if* you'll do the tedious work and others won't. YC funded Stripe, so he'll compare you to Stripe, and that's a high bar.

**What would change his answer:** if you're your own most demanding user, and a handful of agent builders already depend on you and grow week over week, most of this falls away. Then the conversation becomes how to grow faster.

**Gaps:** the vault has nothing from Seibel, Caldwell or PG on AI agents or agentic commerce. Everything on that is applied from his general principles, not something he said.
